theme: Spiritual gifts; one body; love supreme
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 12:1-14:40. These three chapters form one argument about spiritual gifts. Read chapter 13 in its place, not in isolation: it sits between two chapters on gifts and explains how they are to be used. Notice the body in chapter 12, love in chapter 13, and order in chapter 14.
settingTheScene: The Corinthians were eager for spiritual gifts, especially the dramatic ones like tongues. But their use of gifts had become a source of pride, rivalry, and disorder in worship. Paul takes the opportunity to teach about the nature and purpose of the Spirit’s gifts. Chapter 13 is not a stand-alone poem on love for weddings, although it is often read there. It is a rebuke and a remedy for a church that valued display over love.
observation: “No one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit” (12:3).
“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (12:7).
“For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ” (12:12).
“If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together” (12:26).
“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal” (13:1).
“Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude” (13:4).
“So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love” (13:13).
“But all things should be done decently and in order” (14:40).
interpretation:
Paul begins with a test. Pagans were led astray to mute idols. By contrast, “no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says Jesus is accursed, and no one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit.” Every believer has the Spirit, shown by confessing Christ as Lord. Then comes the Trinity: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.” The gifts are for “the common good,” not for private status. Paul lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, distinguishing of spirits, tongues, and interpretation, all empowered by one and the same Spirit, “who apportions to each one individually as he wills.”

He then pictures the church as a body. “Just as the body is one and has many members… so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free.” The foot cannot say it is not part of the body because it is not a hand. The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you.” God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it, that there may be no division. “If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together. Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.” He lists the offices again: apostles, prophets, teachers, miracle workers, healers, helpers, administrators, tongues. “And I will show you a still more excellent way.”

That way is love. Without it, the most impressive gifts are noise. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith that moves mountains, giving all I have, even martyrdom: “if I have not love, I gain nothing.” Then the description: love is patient and kind; does not envy or boast; is not arrogant or rude; does not insist on its own way; is not irritable or resentful; does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Read these as a portrait of Christ, and a mirror for ourselves. “Love never ends.” Prophecies will pass away, tongues will cease, knowledge will vanish. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. “So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.”

Chapter 14 applies the principle. Pursue love, and desire the spiritual gifts, especially prophecy, because it builds up the church. Tongues, unless interpreted, edify only the speaker. “In church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.” The aim is building up. Women and men should keep order: “God is not a God of confusion but of peace.” Verses 34 to 35 on women being silent have been understood in different ways: as a local issue of disruptive questions, as a restriction on weighing prophecy, or as a quotation of a Corinthian slogan. “But all things should be done decently and in order.”
connection: Acts 2 describes the Spirit at Pentecost. Romans 12:3-8 and Ephesians 4:1-16 also treat gifts and the body. John 13:34-35 gives the new commandment of love. Colossians 3:14 says above all put on love. 1 John 4:7-21 says God is love. Galatians 5:22-23 lists the fruit of the Spirit. Matthew 22:37-40 sums up the law as love. 1 Peter 4:10-11 speaks of using gifts to serve others. Philippians 2:1-4 teaches humility. 2 Corinthians 3:18 and 5:7 speak of seeing now and then.
application:
Read chapter 13 and replace the word “love” with your own name. Where does it not fit? Ask Christ, who does fit, to make it true of you.

Ask what gift God gave you for the common good. Offer it this week.

Honor a member of your church who is less visible, like the weaker parts of the body.
prayerPrompts: Thank the Holy Spirit for giving each believer gifts for the common good.
Ask him to make you content as part of the body.
Ask him to make love supreme in your gifts.
